title: Review a TypeScript API client full of unsafe type assertions
description: Problem: Review a TypeScript API client full of unsafe type assertions. Solve this problem with multiple approaches and detailed explanations.

data.text: **Review a TypeScript API client full of unsafe type assertions** is a type-safety review. When an API client uses `as` to force the compiler to accept any shape of data, it bypasses TypeScript's main value: catching mismatches at build time. A senior review should identify every assertion, explain why it is unsafe, and propose a safer pattern such as runtime validation, branded types, or discriminated unions.

items: API responses that changed shape on the server but compile fine because the client casts blindly
Null or undefined fields that crash at runtime when the code assumes they exist
Enum values that the server returns as strings but the client casts to numbers
Array fields that the server returns as objects after a schema migration
Optional fields marked as required with `as Required<T>`
Third-party SDK types that are loosely defined and force the consumer to assert

terms.definition: Using `as` or angle-bracket syntax to tell TypeScript to treat a value as a specific type, bypassing structural checks.
Checking the shape of data at runtime with a library like Zod, Valibot, or Arktype before passing it to typed code.
A nominal type created by adding an opaque brand property to a primitive, preventing accidental mixing of IDs, emails, and slugs.
A union of types that share a common literal property, allowing TypeScript to narrow the type in each branch.
TypeScript's type system is structural: two types are compatible if their shapes match, regardless of their names.

data.text: The typical anti-pattern is a response interceptor that takes raw JSON and asserts it into the expected type. If the server returns an error envelope with a different shape, the assertion succeeds at compile time and the app crashes on the first access to a missing field.

data.title: Unsafe: blind assertion after fetch
data.content: This interceptor casts the response to User without checking the actual shape. Any server change that breaks the User schema will pass the type check and fail at runtime:

data.title: Safer: runtime validation with Zod
data.content: Zod infers a TypeScript type from the schema and validates at runtime. If the response shape changes, the parse throws before the app uses the data:

data.title: Progressive safety
items: Zod, Valibot, or Arktype: schema-based runtime validation that infers static types
Branded types: prevent mixing IDs, slugs, and emails by adding an opaque brand
Discriminated unions: model API variants with a shared tag and narrow in each branch
Generics with constraints: write functions that accept any input but constrain it to a known shape
Satisfies operator: validate that a value satisfies a type without widening its inference
Strict null checks: enable `strictNullChecks` and avoid `!` non-null assertions on API data

cards.title: as assertion
cards.description: Tell TypeScript to trust you without checking.

cards.title: Runtime validation
cards.description: Parse and validate the response against a schema before using it.

cards.title: Branded types
cards.description: Nominal types for primitives that should not be mixed.

cards.title: Discriminated unions
cards.description: Model API variants with a shared tag field.
cons: Requires server to send the tag

data.title: Assertions are not types
data.text: TypeScript types are erased at runtime. An `as User` cast does not transform the data—it only silences the compiler. If the server returns a string instead of a number, the cast succeeds and the app crashes when the code tries to multiply the string.

data.title: Steps to find unsafe assertions
items: Search the codebase for `as ` and `as<` in API client files
For each assertion, ask: what happens if the server returns a different shape?
Replace blind assertions with runtime validation for every external boundary
Use branded types for IDs and other primitives that should not be mixed

data.title: Eliminate unsafe assertions
data.description: Take an API client file that uses `as` to cast fetch responses. Replace every assertion with runtime validation using Zod or Valibot. Verify the app still compiles and behaves correctly.
steps: Find all `as` casts in API response handlers
Define a Zod schema for each endpoint response
Replace the cast with `.parse()` and handle parse errors with a try/catch
Infer the TypeScript type from the schema with `z.infer`
Run the type checker and confirm no new errors
data.expectedOutcome: The API client should validate all incoming data, and any server-side schema change should surface as a parse error before the app uses the data.

items.question: What if the API is a third-party SDK I cannot control?
items.answer: Validate the SDK response at the boundary where it enters your code. Wrap the SDK call in a function that validates the result against your own schema before passing it downstream.

items.question: Does runtime validation hurt performance?
items.answer: Zod and Valibot are fast for typical payload sizes. The cost is negligible compared to a network request. If you are parsing thousands of records per second, benchmark and consider validating only the fields you use.

items.question: What about GraphQL with code generation?
items.answer: Code-generated types are safe as long as the schema and generator are in sync. Validate the generated types against the actual API response in integration tests. If the schema changes without regenerating, the test catches the mismatch.

data.title: Summary
points: Type assertions bypass compile-time safety; they do not validate runtime data
Use runtime validation at every external boundary: fetch, WebSocket, SDK
Zod, Valibot, and similar libraries infer types from schemas, keeping types and validation in sync
Branded types prevent primitive collisions at compile time
Enable strict compiler options to surface unsafe patterns early
data.takeaway: A type-safe API client trusts no data from the network until it has been validated. Assertions are a shortcut that eventually becomes a trap.
